Comment parler sans être instrumentalisé: How to speak out without being used
Alors, quel espace faut-il pour cette pr: So what kind of space does this speaking out need within the Muslim community?
En marge de la Semaine de sensibilisatio: During Muslim Awareness Week, we gave a platform to several Muslim women. What did we find? From every side and every camp, their voices make people uncomfortable. Especially when the subject is the hijab… and taking it off.
Natasha Ivisic en sait quelque chose, el: Natasha Ivisic knows this well. She was invited onto the set of Tout le monde en parle in 2009 for her film Je porte le voile (I Wear the Veil). Today, she no longer wears one.
« Je crois que mon film a permis une mei: “I think my film helped people better understand the topic of the hijab, and the fact that it's a personal journey. But it was also confronting for some people that I took mine off publicly.” After the initial shock, her work was, on the whole, well received. “I always stayed very nuanced, which earned me the respect of the Muslims around me and discouraged the columnists and others who were looking for a polarizing message. That kind of celebrity didn't interest me.”
Natasha Ivisic a tout de même été longte: Still, Natasha Ivisic was consulted by the media for a long time whenever a hijab-related issue made the news.
Depuis, le voile a continué à faire l’ob: Since then, the hijab has continued to be the subject of public reflection and analysis. In 2017, journalist Kenza Bennis's book Les monologues du voile also generated a lot of talk before being very well received.
Et actuellement, un livre à paraître fai: And right now, an upcoming book is getting people talking in Quebec's Muslim community. An excerpt from the back cover of Le vent dans le voile, an autobiographical account by Samah Jebbari*, has caused an uproar because it links taking off the hijab with a personal experience of liberation. Even before knowing what the book contains, some people are worried about the repercussions of its publication.
Essraa Daoui est enseignante, musulmane: Essraa Daoui is a teacher, a Muslim woman who wears the hijab, and someone who has been involved in public debates for several years. For a long time, she believed the best way forward was to break taboos publicly and take firm positions. Over time, her outlook has shifted a little. “Let's just say that today, if I take the trouble to speak out publicly, it's to bring about real change, and after weighing all the possible consequences.”
C’est d’ailleurs ce qu’elle a fait récem: That is what she did recently with a Facebook post that circulated widely. In it, she offers her support and love to her Muslim sisters who have decided to take off their hijab, while urging them not to turn it into a media cause. “It's dangerous because when there's a narrative of oppression around the hijab, only a rare few people will see the nuance and understand that it's a personal story, specific to one person's experience.”
Essraa craint que ce genre de discours n: Essraa fears that this kind of narrative feeds Islamophobia. “Even with COVID, Muslims are still at the centre of the news. Our mental health is already fragile, so yes, the slightest announcement of a book that seems ‘controversial’ is going to be a trigger, even if its author has done nuanced work.”
Au fil des ans, Essraa a remarqué que se: Over the years, Essraa has noticed that her public positions, on subjects ranging from feminism to freedom of expression to the hijab, have only polarized debates. “I got a certain amount of sympathy from people who were happy to finally see a Muslim woman speak up, but who didn't understand the intersection of our oppressions and who, in some cases, used me.
De l’autre côté, je faisais face à une c: On the other side, I had a Muslim community that supported me, but that also dug in when it was being pointed at,” she sums up. She still believes real change can come from sincere debate and criticism, sometimes harsh but necessary. So what kind of space does this speaking out need within the Muslim community? “A safe space,” she answers simply.
Amina (prénom fictif), qui a récemment d: Amina (not her real name), who recently decided to take off the hijab after wearing it for nearly a decade, agrees. She has a lot to say on the subject. “For me, these are questions that need to be analyzed in depth in safe spaces. There are too many nuances to explain, nuances that most people will never understand.” She is quick to point out that if she asked for anonymity for this article, it is not out of fear of reprisals from her community. “I just don't want to be used by those who want to speak against Islam, against the hijab. My story belongs to me.”
Cette peur d’être instrumentalisée est s: This fear of being used came up again and again in the testimonies. “When I took off the hijab, the last thing I wanted was for the Martineaus of this world to claim victory. In fact, their victory is having legitimized everyone who felt entitled to insult me and spit on me in the street. They created a climate of Islamophobia that is too heavy for some Muslim women to bear… women like me.”
Si Amina a réussi à vivre avec le racism: Amina managed to live with racism for several years, but becoming a mother changed how she sees things. She could not bear for her son to witness these micro- and macro-aggressions. “I no longer wear a hijab on my head, but I still carry Islam in my heart. So these Islamophobes will surely run into me at the splash pads at the Granby Zoo, without a hijab but in a burkini.”
Le concept de safe space n’est pas nouve: The concept of the safe space is not new. These “safe spaces” emerged in the mid-1960s in the United States. They reportedly first applied to places frequented by members of the LGBT+ community, then to feminist movements, before extending to other marginalized groups.
Pour Asmaa Ibnouzahir, il est évident qu: For Asmaa Ibnouzahir, it is clear that a new generation of Muslims is looking for alternative spaces to debate or discuss sensitive questions related to their faith or identity. Offering such spaces is in fact one of the missions of her non-profit organization, Institut F, which offers workshops, training and other resources for Muslim women in Quebec.
« J’avoue que, au début, j’étais surpris: “I admit that at first, I was surprised by the age of the members, most of whom are in their early twenties. There's a whole generation of young Muslim women in Quebec who don't see themselves in existing institutions or can't find their voice there.” At Institut F, workshops like RISE (Réflexion sur l'islam, la société et l'empowerment des femmes, or Reflection on Islam, Society and Women's Empowerment) allow Muslim women to analyze religious texts, debate them and reinterpret them free from judgment.
Ces espaces peuvent également être virtu: These spaces can also be virtual, such as private Facebook groups that allow this kind of exchange. During lockdown, they are all the more relevant. In the end, the best space is the one where speech is freed and where change happens.
« Honnêtement, tous les grands discours: “Honestly, all the big speeches and public debates will never be as meaningful to me as a girls' night in a living room, where we talk about the real stuff with no taboos,” concludes Essraa Daoui.
Mais il faut faire attention : les espac: But we need to be careful: safe spaces must not become a brake on freedom of expression by silencing those who want to speak out more publicly. Even if they fear the social repercussions of doing so.
« Oui, nous sommes victimes d’islamophob: “Yes, we are victims of external Islamophobia, but there are also victims among us. We need to support them and let them express their truth the way they want to,” says Nafissah Rahman, an interpreter and activist in Montréal's Bengali community.
Asmaa Ibnouzahir, qui a également fini p: Asmaa Ibnouzahir, who also ended up giving up the hijab, knows something about this. She has made numerous media appearances and published a book, Chroniques d'une musulmane indignée, with Éditions Fides. In it, she takes aim at her own community, among others. “It's not about staying quiet or protecting certain Muslims, who often don't deserve to be protected! But there's a way to approach sensitive subjects that covers every angle,” says the author.
Ainsi, quand elle aborde la question du: So when she addresses sexism in the Muslim community, she makes a point of placing the subject in the broader context of widespread patriarchy. “After all, women's shelters and femicides didn't begin with Muslim immigration.”
Nafissah Rahman abonde dans ce sens. « A: Nafissah Rahman agrees. “No society, no culture is perfect. What becomes exhausting is that we have double the work to do: educating our community and educating the rest of Quebec society.”
Travaillant auprès de femmes musulmanes: Working with Muslim women in vulnerable situations, Nafissah encourages them to speak up, even when it makes people uncomfortable or risks stirring up hatred. “If we're afraid to speak, if we're ashamed to speak, it creates trauma. It's even our responsibility as Muslims to support one another and stand on the side of truth,” says the interpreter.
<strong>Une Semaine de sensibilisation m: A Muslim Awareness Week for more humanity
Samira Laouni est l’une des femmes à l’o: Samira Laouni is one of the women behind Muslim Awareness Week, which takes place every year from January 25 to 31. Launched after the attack on the Québec City mosque in 2017, the initiative aims to be a channel for exchange that is constructive, transparent and, above all, human. “In the end, the central message we want to get across is this: we are all living beings with the same concerns, expectations, aspirations… and challenges,” she says. She also encourages Muslim Quebecers not to fear unduly the scandals that can arise in their community, as in every other.
Geneviève Mercier-Dalphond a participé m: Geneviève Mercier-Dalphond took part Tuesday in the panel “A plural and harmonious society: an achievable ideal?”, organized as part of Muslim Awareness Week. The McGill University doctoral student in religion and philosophy is researching the repercussions of hate crimes on Muslims in Quebec. For her, one thing is certain: the fear is well founded.
« On observe une corrélation entre les p: “We see a correlation between proposed secularism bills, more specifically Bill 21 and the Charter of Values, and the rise in hate crimes. Women (especially those who wear the hijab) tend to be the first and most frequent victims of daily micro-aggressions,” she explains. According to data compiled by Statistics Canada from 2010 to 2018, violent hate crimes committed against Indigenous (45 per cent) and Muslim (45 per cent) populations were more likely to target women.
Mme Mercier-Dalphond rappelle par ailleu: Ms. Mercier-Dalphond also points out that it is hard to get real data on the subject because, most of the time, victims do not report hate crimes.
« Il y a encore beaucoup de travail à fa: “There's still a lot of work to do, and as long as there's Islamophobia, we'll have to defend ourselves against generalizations and accusations. But I'm hopeful that we'll get there by turning away from false scandals and putting our energy into building bridges and launching positive initiatives.”
